implementation_notes: std::clone::Clone is the pattern as a language trait: #[derive(Clone)] implements field-wise clone() for structs and enums, and .clone() is the explicit, type-directed copy (Copy covers types whose clone is a bitwise copy). What 'deep' means is decided by the field types - String, Vec and Box duplicate their allocations, while Rc/Arc only bump a reference count - so no separate clone method or registry is needed for ordinary values. For template-to-entity creation that must mint a new identity, expose a domain method such as instantiate(id) instead of overloading Clone.
pitfalls: Clone is not deep by decree: a derived clone of a struct holding Arc<Mutex<T>> shares the mutable state (the std docs call this out).
Clone is not object-safe because clone() returns Self, so Box<dyn Trait> cannot be cloned without a helper trait.
Cloning Vec/String-heavy values in a hot loop allocates; prefer &T or Arc when sharing is intended, and use clone_from to reuse an existing allocation.

variants.name: clone_box() helper for dyn Trait (polymorphic clones)
variants.implementation_notes: When prototypes must be cloned behind a trait object - the GoF polymorphic case - add a helper trait with fn clone_box(&self) -> Box<dyn Trait>, blanket-implement it for every T: Trait + Clone, and implement Clone for Box<dyn Trait> on top of it. This restores cloning through the interface where Clone itself cannot be used because clone() returns Self. Prefer a closed enum plus #[derive(Clone)] when the set of prototype kinds is known.
pitfalls: The blanket impl needs 'static + Clone on every implementor, which some types cannot satisfy; the helper trait must be in scope where cloning happens.
A manual impl of ShapeClone for a type that is not Clone silently clones the box pointer, not the value.
Trait objects erase the concrete type: callers get Box<dyn Trait> back and must downcast if they need the concrete type.
